course: Daily Broiler Sales: Batch Production System

lessons.title: Introduction and Why It Matters
lessons.body:
Feed is the single largest cost in broiler production, often accounting for 70% or more of your total expenses. If you are selling broilers daily, you must manage feed carefully or you will eat your profits. A broiler eats about 3.5 to 4 kg of feed to reach 2 kg live weight. At a feed price of 500 shillings per kg, that is 1,750 to 2,000 shillings per bird just for feed. If you sell a 2 kg bird for 2,500 shillings, you are left with only 500 to 750 shillings to cover chicks, medication, labour, and profit. That is why a feed budget is not optionalâit is the backbone of your business.

In a batch production system, you raise birds in groups (batches) and sell them daily as they reach market weight. This means you must plan feed purchases for each batch from day one to day sale. Without a budget, you may run out of feed, forcing you to buy expensive small quantities, or you may overbuy and tie up cash that could be used elsewhere. A feed budget helps you know exactly how much feed you need, when you need it, and how much money to set aside.

For example, if you plan to raise 100 broilers, you will need about 350 to 400 kg of feed from day-old to 2 kg. If you buy in 50 kg bags, that is 7 to 8 bags. At 25,000 shillings per bag, you need 175,000 to 200,000 shillings for feed alone. Breaking this down weekly helps you avoid cash flow problems. In week one, chicks eat littleâabout 10 kg total. By week four, they eat about 100 kg. So you can stagger your purchases.

This module will teach you how to calculate feed needs, choose the right feed, store it properly, and stick to a budget. You will learn to avoid common mistakes like overfeeding, underfeeding, and wasting feed. With a good feed budget, you can predict your costs, set your selling price, and ensure you make a profit every day. Remember: the bird that eats well pays well, but only if you control the cost.

lessons.title: Tools and Materials
lessons.body:
To manage feed and your feed budget effectively, you need a few simple tools and materials. You do not need expensive equipment, but you must be organised. First, get a weighing scale. A hanging scale that can weigh up to 50 kg is ideal. You will use it to weigh feed bags, feed portions, and even birds to check growth. A small kitchen scale (0-5 kg) is useful for weighing feed for young chicks. Without a scale, you are guessing, and guessing leads to waste or underfeeding.

Second, you need feed storage containers. Feed must be kept dry and safe from pests. Use plastic drums with tight lids, or metal bins. If you buy feed in bags, keep them on a wooden pallet off the floor to prevent moisture. Never store feed directly on the ground. Also, get a scoop or container that you use only for feed. A 1-litre plastic cup or a tin can works well. Know how much it holdsâfor example, a 1-litre cup holds about 0.5 kg of feed. This helps you measure without weighing every time.

Third, you need a record book and a pen. This is your feed budget tool. Record every feed purchase: date, quantity, cost, and supplier. Also record daily feed consumption per batch. A simple notebook is fine. You can draw a table with columns for date, batch number, feed given (kg), and notes. At the end of the week, add up the feed used and compare with your budget. This record will show you if you are on track or overspending.

Fourth, you need a calculator or a phone with a calculator. You will do simple maths: multiply feed price by quantity, divide total feed by number of birds, etc. If you have a smartphone, you can use a notes app or a simple spreadsheet. But a paper record is more reliable in areas with no electricity.

Finally, consider a feed mixer if you plan to mix your own feed. This can save money, but only if you can source ingredients cheaply and mix correctly. For beginners, buying complete feed from a reputable supplier is safer. You will also need a wheelbarrow or bucket to carry feed to the pens. Keep all tools clean and in one place. A well-organised feed corner saves time and prevents mistakes.

lessons.title: Step by Step Method
lessons.body:
Step 1: Calculate total feed needed for your batch. Decide how many birds you will raise and to what weight. For broilers, a good target is 2 kg live weight at 6 weeks. On average, a broiler eats 3.8 kg of feed to reach 2 kg. So for 100 birds, you need 100 x 3.8 = 380 kg of feed. Round up to 400 kg to be safe. If you buy 50 kg bags, that is 8 bags.

Step 2: Break down feed by week. Broilers eat differently each week. Here is a typical weekly feed intake per bird: Week 1: 0.15 kg, Week 2: 0.4 kg, Week 3: 0.7 kg, Week 4: 1.0 kg, Week 5: 1.2 kg, Week 6: 1.35 kg. Total = 4.8 kg? That is too high. Actually, these are cumulative? Let me correct: For 100 birds, weekly total feed: Week 1: 15 kg, Week 2: 40 kg, Week 3: 70 kg, Week 4: 100 kg, Week 5: 120 kg, Week 6: 135 kg. Total = 480 kg. That is for 2.5 kg? I need to be accurate. Common figures: A broiler eats about 1 kg feed per 0.5 kg gain? No, feed conversion ratio (FCR) is about 1.8. So for 2 kg gain, feed = 3.6 kg. For 100 birds, 360 kg. Weekly: Week 1: 10 kg, Week 2: 30 kg, Week 3: 60 kg, Week 4: 90 kg, Week 5: 100 kg, Week 6: 70 kg. Sum = 360 kg. Let's use that. So plan to buy 7 bags (350 kg) and adjust.

Step 3: Cost the feed. Find the current price per bag. Suppose a 50 kg bag costs 25,000 shillings. Total feed cost = 7 x 25,000 = 175,000 shillings. Add 10% for price changes and waste = 192,500 shillings. This is your feed budget for the batch.

Step 4: Schedule purchases. Do not buy all feed at once. Buy week 1 and 2 feed (40 kg) at the start. Then buy week 3 and 4 feed (150 kg) at the end of week 2. Buy week 5 and 6 feed (170 kg) at the end of week 4. This spreads your cash outlay.

Step 5: Measure and feed daily. Use your scoop to give the right amount. For 100 birds in week 1, each bird eats 0.15 kg? Actually, 10 kg total for 100 birds = 0.1 kg per bird per day? No, 10 kg for the week = 1.4 kg per day for 100 birds = 14 g per bird per day. That is too low. Let's recalc: Week 1 total 10 kg for 100 birds = 0.1 kg per bird for the week = 14 g per day. That seems low. Typical day-old chicks eat about 10-15 g per day in first week. So 100 birds eat 1-1.5 kg per day. Over 7 days, 7-10 kg. So 10 kg is fine. So daily feed: Week 1: 1.5 kg/day, Week 2: 4 kg/day, Week 3: 8.5 kg/day, Week 4: 13 kg/day, Week 5: 14 kg/day, Week 6: 10 kg/day. Adjust based on consumption.

Step 6: Record and review. Every day, note how much feed you gave. At the end of the week, compare with your plan. If you used more, find out why. Adjust next week. Keep your budget updated.

lessons.title: Common Mistakes and Fixes
lessons.body:
Mistake 1: Not keeping feed records. Many farmers feed by guesswork and never write down how much they use. This leads to running out of feed or overspending. Fix: Keep a daily feed log. Write the date, batch, and amount given. At the end of the week, add it up. Compare with your budget. If you are using more than planned, investigate.

Mistake 2: Buying feed in small quantities. When you run out and buy a few kilograms from a local shop, you pay a higher price per kg. Fix: Plan your purchases. Buy in 50 kg bags from a supplier. If cash is tight, join with other farmers to buy in bulk and share the discount.

Mistake 3: Overfeeding. Some farmers think more feed means faster growth. But broilers have limited capacity. Overfeeding wastes feed and can cause health problems like ascites. Fix: Follow the feeding guide. Use a scale to weigh feed for the first two weeks. After that, use a scoop and stick to the recommended daily amount. If birds leave feed in the trough, reduce the amount.

Mistake 4: Underfeeding. This is worse because birds will not reach market weight on time, and you will sell at a loss. Fix: Monitor bird weight weekly. Weigh a few birds (5-10) each week. If they are below target, increase feed slightly. But do not overdo it.

Mistake 5: Poor storage. Feed that gets wet or is attacked by rats is money lost. Fix: Store feed in a dry, raised place. Use airtight containers. Keep only one week's feed in the poultry house. The rest stays in the store. Rotate stock: use older feed first.

Mistake 6: Not adjusting for feed price changes. Feed prices fluctuate. If you budgeted at 25,000 per bag and the price rises to 28,000, your budget is off. Fix: Check prices weekly. Keep a buffer of 10% in your budget. If prices rise, adjust your selling price or find a cheaper supplier.

Mistake 7: Feeding the wrong feed. Broilers need different feed at different stages: starter (0-4 weeks), grower (4-6 weeks), and finisher (6 weeks to market). Using the wrong feed wastes money. Fix: Buy the correct feed for each stage. Label your storage clearly.

Mistake 8: Not accounting for mortality. If birds die, you need less feed. But many farmers keep feeding the same amount. Fix: Adjust feed after any mortality. If you lose 5 birds out of 100, reduce feed by 5%.

By avoiding these mistakes, you will keep your feed budget on track and your profits healthy.

lessons.title: Safety and Best Practice
lessons.body:
Safety in feed management is about protecting your health, your birds, and your money. First, personal safety. Feed dust can cause breathing problems. Always wear a dust mask when handling feed, especially when mixing or scooping. Wash your hands after handling feed, especially before eating. Keep feed away from children and pets. Store feed in a locked area if possible.

Second, feed safety. Feed can carry bacteria like Salmonella. Never use mouldy or spoiled feed. Mould produces toxins that can kill your birds. If feed smells sour or has clumps, do not use it. Keep feed dry. Moisture leads to mould and spoilage. Store feed in a cool, dry place. Use pallets to keep bags off the floor. Close bags tightly after opening. Use opened bags within one week.

Third, bird safety. Feed must be fresh and free of contaminants. Do not use feed that has been spilled on the floor and swept upâit may contain droppings or dirt. Use clean feeders. Clean feeders daily to prevent feed buildup. Remove any wet or caked feed. Provide enough feeder space so birds do not crowd. A good rule: 5 cm of feeder space per bird. For 100 birds, you need 5 metres of feeder length. If feeders are too small, some birds will not get enough feed.

Fourth, best practices for feed budgeting. Keep a separate bank account or cash box for feed money. Do not mix feed money with personal money. Buy feed from reputable suppliers who provide quality feed. Ask for a receipt. Check the manufacturing date on the bag. Use feed within three months of manufacturing. Weigh feed for the first two weeks to calibrate your scoop. Then you can rely on the scoop. But re-calibrate if you change feed type or supplier.

Fifth, environmental safety. Store feed away from chemicals like pesticides or fuel. These can contaminate feed and poison your birds. Keep feed storage clean and free of rodents. Use traps, not poison, near feed. If you must use poison, place it far from feed.

Sixth, financial safety. Your feed budget should include a contingency of 10% for price increases or unexpected needs. Review your budget weekly. If you are overspending, find out why and fix it. Do not borrow money for feed unless you are sure of your selling price. Remember, feed is your biggest costâprotect it like your life.

lessons.title: Practical Exercise
lessons.body:
Now it is time to put what you have learned into practice. This exercise will help you create a feed budget for a batch of 100 broilers. Follow these steps and write your answers in your record book.

Step 1: Calculate total feed needed. Assume you will raise 100 broilers to 2 kg live weight. Using the average feed conversion ratio of 1.8, calculate total feed: 100 birds x 2 kg x 1.8 = 360 kg. Round up to 400 kg to be safe. How many 50 kg bags is that? 400 / 50 = 8 bags.

Step 2: Find the current feed price. Call your local feed supplier or visit the market. Ask for the price of broiler starter, grower, and finisher. For this exercise, assume starter costs 26,000 per 50 kg bag, grower costs 25,000, and finisher costs 24,000. You will need: Starter for weeks 1-4: about 200 kg (4 bags). Grower for weeks 4-6: about 120 kg (2.4 bags, so 3 bags). Finisher for week 6 to market: about 80 kg (1.6 bags, so 2 bags). Total bags: 4+3+2 = 9 bags. But you only need 8 bags total. Adjust: use 3 bags starter, 3 bags grower, 2 bags finisher = 8 bags. Calculate total cost: 3 x 26,000 = 78,000; 3 x 25,000 = 75,000; 2 x 24,000 = 48,000. Total = 201,000 shillings.

Step 3: Add a 10% contingency. 201,000 x 0.10 = 20,100. Total budget = 221,100 shillings.

Step 4: Schedule purchases. Week 1: buy 1 bag starter (26,000). Week 2: buy 1 bag starter (26,000). Week 3: buy 1 bag starter and 1 bag grower (51,000). Week 4: buy 1 bag grower (25,000). Week 5: buy 1 bag grower and 1 bag finisher (49,000). Week 6: buy 1 bag finisher (24,000). Total = 201,000. This spreads your cash outlay.

Step 5: Daily feeding plan. For 100 birds, daily feed: Week 1: 1.5 kg/day. Week 2: 4 kg/day. Week 3: 8.5 kg/day. Week 4: 13 kg/day. Week 5: 14 kg/day. Week 6: 10 kg/day. Use a scale to measure feed for the first week. Then use a scoop that you have calibrated. For example, if 1 scoop = 0.5 kg, then week 1 you give 3 scoops per day.

Step 6: Record and review. For one week, record daily feed given. At the end of the week, compare with the plan. If you used more, check for spillage or overfeeding. If you used less, check if birds are underweight. Adjust as needed.

Step 7: Calculate your break-even selling price. If total feed cost is 221,100, and you have other costs (chicks, medication, labour) of 100,000, total cost = 321,100. If you expect 95 birds to survive, cost per bird = 321,100 / 95 = 3,380 shillings. To make a 20% profit, selling price per bird = 3,380 x 1.20 = 4,056 shillings. So you must sell each bird for at least 4,100 shillings to be safe.

Write all these calculations in your record book. This is your feed budget. Keep it safe and refer to it daily.

lessons.title: Practical Reference
lessons.body:
Practical Reference: Feed and the Feed Budget for Daily Broiler Sales

In a daily broiler sales operation, feed is not a cost line â it is the engine of your batch calendar. Every day you delay a sale, every gram of feed wasted, and every bird that dies before market weight directly reduces the money that lands in your pocket. This Practical Reference lesson gives you the numbers, tools, and habits you need to build a feed budget that protects your margin from day-old chick to final sale.

Broiler production in Africa is dominated by small and medium-scale producers who sell live birds daily to local markets, restaurants, and households. Feed typically represents 65â75% of total variable production cost. If you cannot forecast feed need and cost per bird, you cannot price your birds correctly, and you cannot know whether a batch is profitable until it is too late. This module is about turning feed from a guess into a controlled, budgeted input.

Why the Feed Budget Is a Business Tool, Not a Farm Chore

A feed budget answers four questions every day:

  1. How much feed do my birds need today, this week, and until sale?
  2. How much will that feed cost at current market prices?
  3. What is my feed cost per bird and per kilogram of live weight?
  4. When will I run out of feed, and what is my reorder point?

In practice, many farmers buy feed reactively â when the bag is empty. This creates two problems: emergency purchases at higher prices, and feed outages that stall growth. A feed budget converts these emergencies into planned purchases, which often means better prices, fewer transport trips, and a batch that reaches market weight on schedule.

Key Performance Indicators for Broiler Feed

Before building the budget, you need baseline figures. The table below shows typical performance ranges for broilers under tropical and sub-tropical African conditions, based on published extension and research data.

Table 1: Typical Broiler Feed and Performance Benchmarks (Africa Context)
Parameter Starter (0â4 weeks) Finisher (4â6 weeks) Total (to 2.0â2.2 kg live weight)
Feed intake per bird 1.6â1.9 kg 2.8â3.2 kg 4.4â5.1 kg
Feed Conversion Ratio (FCR) 1.6â1.8 2.0â2.3 2.0â2.3
Mortality (acceptable range) 2â4% 1â3% 3â6%
Feed cost share of total cost â â 65â75%
Sources: FAO Animal Production and Health Manual (Poultry Development); ILRI Smallholder Poultry Production technical notes; AIC (Agri-Information Centre) broiler extension guidelines.

These are benchmarks, not guarantees. Local climate, breed, feed quality, and management will shift the numbers. Your job is to measure your own flock and compare against these ranges. If your FCR is above 2.5, you are losing money on every bird.

Building a Simple Feed Budget

The feed budget is a planning table. You multiply the number of birds by expected feed intake, then multiply by the price per kilogram of feed. The table below shows a worked example for a 200-bird batch in a typical African market context.

Table 2: Worked Feed Budget for a 200-Bird Broiler Batch (6-Week Cycle)
Item Quantity per bird Total for 200 birds Unit price (USD, indicative) Total cost (USD)
Starter feed (0â4 weeks) 1.8 kg 360 kg 0.55 / kg 198.00
Finisher feed (4â6 weeks) 3.0 kg 600 kg 0.50 / kg 300.00
Total feed 4.8 kg 960 kg â 498.00
Day-old chicks (200) â 200 birds 0.80 / chick 160.00
Vaccines & medication â â â 40.00
Labour & utilities â â â 60.00
Total variable cost â â â 758.00
Expected live weight (2.0 kg Ã 190 birds) â 380 kg 2.60 / kg 988.00
Gross margin â â â 230.00
Note: Prices are indicative for planning only. Replace with current local market prices. Mortality assumed at 5% (190 birds sold). Sources: FAO Poultry Sector Review; ILRI market price surveys; national agriculture extension cost guides.

This table is the heart of your daily sales operation. If feed price rises by 10%, your gross margin falls by roughly 20%. That is why the feed budget is not a one-time calculation â it must be updated every time feed prices change or your flock performance shifts.

Feed Conversion Ratio: The Number That Decides Profit

FCR is calculated as:

FCR = Total feed consumed (kg) Ã· Total live weight gained (kg)

If a bird eats 4.8 kg and reaches 2.0 kg, FCR = 2.4. If it eats 4.4 kg and reaches 2.2 kg, FCR = 2.0. The difference is 0.4 kg of feed per bird â on a 200-bird batch, that is 80 kg of feed, which at USD 0.50/kg is USD 40. That is real money. Improving FCR is the fastest way to improve margin without raising prices.

Feed Storage and Loss Control

Feed that is stored badly is feed you paid for but never fed. In humid African climates, feed can spoil within weeks. Key practices:

  • Store feed on pallets, never directly on the floor.
  • Keep bags at least 10 cm from walls to allow air circulation.
  • Use the oldest feed first (FIFO â First In, First Out).
  • Keep storage dry and ventilated; mouldy feed causes disease and rejection.
  • Protect against rodents and birds, which consume and contaminate feed.

Feed loss of 5% on a 960 kg batch is 48 kg â nearly USD 25. Over a year of batches, this is a significant and preventable loss.

Feed Budget and Daily Sales: The Connection

In a daily broiler sales model, you are not selling all birds at once. You sell a few birds each day as they reach market weight. This means your feed budget must be dynamic: birds remaining in the house still need feed, while sold birds stop consuming. The practical approach is to recalculate feed need every week based on the number of birds remaining and their average weight.

A simple weekly feed budget:

  • Count remaining birds.
  • Estimate average weight (weigh a sample of 10 birds).
  • Use the benchmark intake table to estimate feed for the coming week.
  • Compare with feed in store; order the difference.

This prevents both overstocking feed (which ties up cash and risks spoilage) and understocking (which stalls growth and delays sales).

Practical Exercise

Using the tables above, complete the following for your own operation:

  1. Enter your current batch size and expected sale weight.
  2. Using Table 1, calculate total feed needed for the batch.
  3. Using your local feed price, calculate total feed cost.
  4. Calculate feed cost per bird and feed cost per kg of live weight.
  5. Compare your FCR with the benchmark range. If above 2.5, identify one management change to improve it.
  6. Set a reorder point: the number of bags at which you must place a new order to avoid running out.

â ï¸ Safety Warning: Feed and Chemical Hazards

Never store feed in the same room as pesticides, herbicides, or veterinary drugs. Feed absorbs chemical vapours and can become toxic to birds and, through meat, to consumers. Always store feed in a dedicated, dry, ventilated space. When using medicated feed or adding drugs to feed, wear gloves and a mask, follow withdrawal periods strictly, and record all treatments. Selling birds before the withdrawal period ends can leave drug residues in meat and is illegal in most countries.

Quick Reference Checklist

  • Know your FCR. Measure feed in and weight gained. Target 2.0â2.3 for broilers to 2.0â2.2 kg.
  • Calculate feed cost per bird before you set your selling price. If feed cost per bird is USD 2.50 and you sell at USD 2.60, you are losing money.
  • Update the feed budget weekly as birds are sold and feed prices change.
  • Set a reorder point. Never let feed drop below one week's requirement.
  • Store feed correctly. Pallets, ventilation, FIFO, no chemicals nearby.
  • Weigh a sample of birds weekly to track growth and detect problems early.
  • Record every bag in and every bag fed. If the numbers do not match, investigate.
  • Review mortality and culls. Dead birds still consumed feed â they are a direct loss.

Further Reading (Free Official Sources)

  • FAO â Poultry Production and Products: Global guidance on small-scale poultry production, feed, and health.
  • ILRI â Smallholder Poultry Research: Technical notes on feeding, breeds, and market access in Africa.
  • CGIAR â Improving Smallholder Poultry Production in Africa: Research summaries on feed efficiency and profitability.
  • South Africa Department of Agriculture â Broiler Production Guidelines: Practical extension materials on broiler management and feed.
  • FAO â Poultry Sector Review (PDF): Detailed data on feed costs, FCR, and market systems in developing countries.

Business-first takeaway: Your feed budget is your profit plan. If you know your feed cost per bird and your FCR, you know your margin before you sell a single chicken. If you do not, you are guessing â and in daily broiler sales, guessing is expensive.

quiz.q: What percentage of total broiler production cost is typically taken up by feed?
quiz.explanation: Feed is the largest cost in broiler production, often accounting for 70% or more of total expenses.

quiz.q: What is the average feed conversion ratio (FCR) for broilers?
quiz.explanation: A typical FCR for broilers is about 1.8, meaning 1.8 kg of feed produces 1 kg of live weight gain.

quiz.q: Why is a feed budget important in a batch production system?
options: A) It helps you know how much feed you need, when to buy, and how much money to set aside.
B) It allows you to feed birds more often.
C) It eliminates the need for record keeping.
D) It guarantees higher selling prices.
quiz.explanation: A feed budget helps plan feed purchases, manage cash flow, and control costs.

quiz.q: Which tool is essential for accurately measuring feed, especially for young chicks?
quiz.explanation: A weighing scale ensures you feed the correct amount, preventing waste or underfeeding.

quiz.q: How should feed be stored to prevent spoilage?
options: A) On the floor in open bags
B) In a dry, raised place in airtight containers
C) Near chemicals for easy access
D) In a wet area to keep it cool
quiz.explanation: Feed must be kept dry and off the floor to prevent moisture, pests, and mould.

quiz.q: What is a good record-keeping practice for feed management?
options: A) Only record feed purchases, not daily use.
B) Record daily feed consumption per batch.
D) Record only when you run out of feed.
quiz.explanation: Recording daily feed consumption helps track usage, compare with budget, and spot problems.

quiz.q: For 100 broilers reaching 2 kg, how many 50 kg bags of feed are needed if total feed is 400 kg?
quiz.explanation: 400 kg divided by 50 kg per bag equals 8 bags.

quiz.q: What is the correct sequence of broiler feed types?
quiz.explanation: Broilers need starter (0-4 weeks), grower (4-6 weeks), and finisher (6 weeks to market).

quiz.q: Why should you avoid buying feed in small quantities frequently?
options: B) It costs more per kg.
quiz.explanation: Buying in small quantities usually means a higher price per kg compared to bulk bags.

quiz.q: What is a common mistake that leads to wasted feed?
quiz.explanation: Overfeeding wastes feed and can cause health problems; birds should be fed according to guidelines.

quiz.q: How can you adjust your feed budget for mortality?
options: A) Ignore mortality; feed the same amount.
B) Increase feed for remaining birds.
C) Reduce feed proportionally to the number of dead birds.
quiz.explanation: If birds die, you need less feed, so reduce the amount to match the remaining flock.

quiz.q: What should you do if feed prices rise after you have set your budget?
options: A) Continue with the same budget.
B) Adjust your selling price or find a cheaper supplier.
D) Buy less feed and underfeed.
quiz.explanation: Feed price changes affect your budget; you must adjust selling price or source cheaper feed to maintain profit.

quiz.q: Why is it important to wear a dust mask when handling feed?
options: B) To prevent breathing problems from feed dust
C) To avoid getting feed on your clothes
D) To make you work faster
quiz.explanation: Feed dust can cause respiratory issues, so a mask protects your health.

quiz.q: What is a sign that feed is spoiled and should not be used?
options: A) It is dry and crumbly
B) It smells sour or has clumps
C) It is a uniform colour
D) It is in a sealed bag
quiz.explanation: Sour smell or clumps indicate mould or bacterial growth, which can harm birds.

quiz.q: How much feeder space is recommended per bird?
quiz.explanation: About 5 cm of feeder space per bird ensures all birds can eat without crowding.

quiz.q: Why should you keep feed money separate from personal money?
options: B) To avoid spending feed money on personal needs
C) To hide it from thieves
D) To make it easier to count
quiz.explanation: Separating funds helps ensure you always have money for feed and do not mix business with personal expenses.

quiz.q: What is a good practice when buying feed?
options: A) Buy from any supplier without checking
B) Check the manufacturing date and ask for a receipt
C) Buy the cheapest feed regardless of quality
D) Buy feed that is past its expiry date
quiz.explanation: Checking the date ensures freshness, and a receipt helps with record keeping and accountability.

quiz.q: How often should you review your feed budget?
options: C) Only when you run out of feed
quiz.explanation: Weekly reviews help you stay on track, spot overspending, and adjust as needed.

quiz.q: In the practical exercise, what is the total feed budget after adding a 10% contingency?
quiz.explanation: 201,000 plus 10% (20,100) equals 221,100 shillings.

quiz.q: What is the break-even selling price per bird if total cost is 321,100 shillings for 95 birds?
quiz.explanation: 321,100 divided by 95 equals approximately 3,380 shillings per bird.

quiz.q: Why is it important to calibrate your feed scoop?
options: A) To make it look nice
B) To ensure you give the correct amount of feed without weighing daily
D) To save time on cleaning
quiz.explanation: Calibrating helps you know how much feed your scoop holds, so you can feed accurately without a scale each time.

quiz.q: What should you do if birds leave feed in the trough?
quiz.explanation: Leftover feed indicates overfeeding; reduce the amount to avoid waste.

quiz.q: How can you prevent rodents from contaminating feed?
options: B) Store feed in airtight containers and use traps
C) Leave feed open for easy access
D) Store feed on the floor
quiz.explanation: Airtight containers and traps keep rodents away without risking poison contamination.

quiz.q: What is the recommended daily feed for 100 birds in week 3?
quiz.explanation: In week 3, 100 birds consume about 8.5 kg per day.

quiz.q: Why should you not feed birds with feed swept from the floor?
options: A) It is dirty and may contain droppings or contaminants
quiz.explanation: Swept feed can be contaminated with droppings, dirt, or pathogens, risking bird health.

quiz.q: What is a benefit of buying feed in bulk?
options: C) More frequent trips to market
quiz.explanation: Bulk buying usually reduces the cost per kg compared to small purchases.

quiz.q: What should you do if you notice birds are underweight at weekly weighing?
options: C) Change to a cheaper feed
quiz.explanation: Underweight birds may need more feed to reach target weight, but increase gradually.

quiz.q: How does a feed budget help with cash flow?
options: A) It ties up all your cash at once.
B) It allows you to stagger purchases and avoid cash shortages.
C) It eliminates the need for record keeping.
quiz.explanation: By planning purchases over time, you can manage cash flow and avoid running out of money or feed.

quiz.q: What is the first step in creating a feed budget?
options: B) Calculate total feed needed for your batch
quiz.explanation: You must know how much feed you need before you can budget for it.

quiz.q: Why is it important to keep feed records even if you have a good memory?
options: A) Records are required by law.
B) Records provide accurate data for decision-making and budgeting.
quiz.explanation: Accurate records help you track usage, compare with budget, and make informed adjustments.
